summary:
Spacey — Space Biology Knowledge Engine

Summary

Spacey is a research prototype that helps students and researchers explore space biology literature through natural-language search and evidence-linked answers. We developed a web interface and API connecting publication discovery, semantic retrieval, and a graph of scientific claims. The ingestion pipeline uses NASA’s Space Biosciences publications page, enriches records through PubMed and Crossref, and stores publication excerpts and extracted claims for exploration.

Users can search topics such as microgravity and bone density, inspect supporting excerpts, ask questions, and explore opposing claim directions and relative research coverage. Local language models support embeddings, claim extraction, and citation-backed answer generation.

Spacey aims to make space biology research easier to navigate and compare. Its claim counts and coverage indicators are exploratory measures, rather than validated assessments of evidence quality or mission readiness.
details:
Spacey combines semantic search, evidence-linked Q&A, and graph exploration in a space biology research interface.

The ingestion service discovers publication links from NASA’s Space Biosciences publications page and retrieves available titles, abstracts, and metadata through PubMed and Crossref. Qdrant stores text embeddings for retrieval, while Neo4j connects publications, excerpts, and extracted claims. Ollama supplies local models for embeddings, claim extraction, and answer generation.

The interface uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SWR, and Vega-Lite. The Python backend uses FastAPI, and Docker Compose coordinates the services.

The creative approach connects relevant excerpts with structured claim relationships, helping users investigate findings and opposing directions while retaining access to source material. Intended benefits include easier literature navigation and comparison; improvements in research speed or accuracy have not yet been measured.

The prototype requires further validation. Generated answers and claims need source review, consensus values are claim counts, coverage describes observed combinations, and mission cards remain examples.
